headline: Edinburgh's Rush Hour: Bicycles Finally Beat Cars
meta_description: For the first time ever, bicycles outnumbered cars during Edinburgh's morning rush hour, driven by e-bike rentals and new segregated cycle lanes.
summary_short: Bicycles outnumbered cars during Edinburgh's morning rush hour for the first time in history, thanks to e-bikes and new cycle infrastructure.
body:
For the first time in history, bicycles outnumbered cars during Edinburgh's morning commute on Leith Walk between 8 and 9 a.m. The milestone reflects a remarkable shift in urban mobility across Scotland's two largest cities, driven by a surge in e-bike rentals and investment in segregated cycling infrastructure. A May traffic survey revealed that bicycle journeys across urban Scotland jumped 25 percent year-over-year, with 67,000 bike trips recorded over just 48 hours. Since the e-bike rental program launched last September, riders have made 1.46 million trips—evidence of what local reporting has called "overwhelming popularity."

The transformation extends beyond Edinburgh's historic streets. In Glasgow, multiple routes now see record cycling traffic, with Victoria Road recording bicycles as 16 percent of all traffic. Kirsty Milton-Moir, a National Health Service health visitor in Glasgow, discovered that cycling not only saves time on her daily rounds visiting families but has fundamentally changed how she works. "Cycling is much quicker than driving," she explained, "and it gives you the headspace you need." Equally important to her is the security that segregated lanes provide—knowing that cyclists have protected space separate from cars has made her commute feel genuinely safe.

Scottish transport officials view these numbers as validation of their infrastructure investment. Cabinet Secretary Stephen Flynn noted that record usage on routes like Glasgow's South City Way and Edinburgh's City Centre West-East Link demonstrates that "infrastructure we are providing is helping more people than ever travel by bike for everyday journeys." With an additional $280 million in mobility projects still in development, Scotland's shift toward cycling shows no sign of slowing.
quick_facts: Edinburgh's Leith Walk: bikes outnumbered cars, 8-9 a.m., May 2024
E-bike program: 1.46 million trips since September launch
Bicycle journeys up 25% year-over-year across urban Scotland
Victoria Road, Glasgow: bikes represent 16% of all traffic
$280 million in additional cycling infrastructure projects planned
